name: Heartburn & reflux
tagline: Common. Treatable. When it is something more.

what_is_it.heading: Heartburn and reflux in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest or throat caused by stomach acid flowing backwards into the food pipe. When it happens often, it is called GORD (gastro-oesophageal reflux disease).
paragraphs: The valve between the stomach and food pipe is meant to stay closed. When it relaxes too often or too long, acid escapes upwards. Result: a hot, burning sensation behind the breastbone — often after meals, often worse lying down.

Occasional heartburn after a big meal is normal. Heartburn that happens twice a week or more, or that wakes you at night, deserves attention. It can damage the food pipe over years. The good news: lifestyle changes plus simple medications work very well for most people.

items.headline: 1 in 4
items.body: South Africans experience heartburn at least once a week. Far more have it occasionally. It is very common.

items.headline: Treatable
items.body: Lifestyle changes plus simple medication (PPIs like omeprazole) work very well. Most people get significant relief within 2 weeks.

items.headline: Can mimic heart
items.body: Severe heartburn can feel like a heart attack. When in doubt — especially with sweating, breathlessness, jaw or arm pain — assume heart and call 10177.

items.headline: Watch for red flags
items.body: Difficulty swallowing, weight loss, vomiting blood, black stools — these are not heartburn. See a doctor without delay.

pull_quote.text: If you are taking heartburn medication every day for more than a few weeks, get a proper assessment. Long-term acid reflux can damage the food pipe and rarely lead to cancer — both preventable with the right care.

signs.heading: What to look out for
signs.lede: Heartburn has a typical pattern — but some symptoms warn of something more serious.

items.title: Typical heartburn
items.description: Burning behind the breastbone, often after meals. Sour or bitter taste at the back of the throat. Worse lying down, bending, or after big or fatty meals. Relief from antacids.

items.title: Reflux features
items.description: Acid coming up into the throat or mouth, especially at night. Persistent cough or hoarseness. Sometimes wheezing or asthma-like symptoms. Worse with weight gain or pregnancy.

items.title: Red flags — see a doctor
items.description: Difficulty or painful swallowing, food sticking, weight loss, vomiting blood, black tarry stools, severe chest pain — possible heart attack. None of these are 'just heartburn'.

myths.heading: What is true and what is not

items.fact: Milk briefly buffers acid, then often makes things worse — milk fat causes more acid release. Use antacids designed for the job (e.g. Gaviscon).

items.myth: Reflux is just discomfort — it doesn't cause real damage.
items.fact: Years of untreated reflux can damage the food pipe lining (oesophagitis), cause narrowing, and rarely lead to a precancerous condition. Worth treating, not just enduring.

items.myth: Heartburn is always after eating spicy food.
items.fact: Common triggers vary: coffee, fatty foods, chocolate, alcohol, peppermint, citrus, large meals, late eating. Different people have different triggers. A food diary helps.

items.myth: If I lose weight, the heartburn will magically go.
items.fact: Weight loss does help significantly, especially around the waist. But many slim people have reflux too — and weight isn't the only factor. Combine weight management with other changes.

prevention.heading: Daily habits that help
prevention.lede: Lifestyle changes are often more powerful than medication for mild to moderate reflux. Worth trying for 4 weeks before settling on pills forever.

items.title: Smaller meals, eat slowly
items.description: Big meals overfill the stomach and push acid up. Try smaller portions, eat slowly, don't go back for seconds at the same sitting.

items.title: Don't eat within 3 hours of bed
items.description: Lying down with a full stomach is a recipe for night reflux. Last meal at least 3 hours before bed. Light snack only if needed.

items.title: Raise the head of the bed
items.description: Put 10–15cm blocks under the headboard legs (not just extra pillows — these bend the neck). Gravity keeps acid down at night.

items.title: Cut your triggers
items.description: Common: coffee, alcohol, fatty foods, chocolate, peppermint, citrus, spicy food, smoking, tight waistbands. Stop smoking entirely — it weakens the valve directly.

items.title: Try lifestyle changes for 4 weeks
items.description: Smaller meals, no late eating, raised bed, identify triggers. About half of people get major relief from these alone — no medication needed.

items.title: Try over-the-counter antacids for occasional
items.description: Gaviscon, Rennies, or similar work quickly for occasional episodes. Available at any pharmacy. Don't use them every day — that's a sign you need a different approach.

items.title: If symptoms 2+ times a week — see a clinic
items.description: PPIs (omeprazole, esomeprazole) used for 4–8 weeks are often very effective. Free at government clinics. Don't take them forever without medical review.

items.title: If red flags appear — go without delay
items.description: Difficulty swallowing, weight loss, vomiting blood, black stools — these need urgent assessment, sometimes endoscopy. Don't try over-the-counter treatment for these.

items.title: If chest pain — assume heart first
items.description: Heart attack and heartburn can feel similar. With sweating, breathlessness, jaw or arm pain, or any uncertainty — call 10177. Better safe.

get_help.heading: Where to go
get_help.lede: Most reflux can be managed at clinic level. Persistent symptoms or red flags benefit from specialist referral.
